title: Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares
summary:
SMB and Windows administrative shares provide file and named pipe access over the Server Message Block protocol, and the administrative shares that exist on Windows systems by default can be used both to move files to a remote host and to request remote execution of a service or scheduled task. An adversary with administrative credentials can copy a payload to a target, then trigger execution through a remote service control or task scheduling interface, and finally clean up the staged file. Because the underlying protocol is the same one used for ordinary file sharing, the traffic does not look unusual at the network layer, and command-line administrative tools are also entirely normal on managed systems.

The reliable evidence is a combination of authentication, share access, and service or task state changes. Destination hosts log network logons and, where detailed file share auditing is enabled, the specific share and path accessed together with the accessing account. Service creation and task registration events on the target record the moment execution was requested, including the binary path referenced, which frequently points at an administrative share path or a temporary directory. Process creation on the target shows what actually ran and under which account, and named pipe access may appear in telemetry from security tooling or from the endpoint agent. On the source side, administrative command execution produces process events that name remote hosts and share paths.

Legitimate configuration management, patching, and backup products use exactly these mechanisms, often at high volume. Effective triage requires knowing which accounts and hosts are authorised to perform remote administration and at what times. Signals that raise confidence include a single account authenticating to many hosts in rapid succession, service creation referencing binaries in user-writable locations, administration activity outside deployment windows, and correlation with an earlier credential access alert.
objectives: Explain how administrative shares, remote service creation, and scheduled task registration combine to produce remote execution.
Interpret share access auditing and service or task creation records on the destination host to confirm execution.
Build a baseline of authorised administrative accounts and hosts to reduce false positives from management tooling.
Detect anomalous fan-out patterns where one account authenticates to many hosts in a short interval.
Explain what evidence survives on the source host and what must be recovered from the target or network capture.
Map SMB-based lateral movement to ATT&CK and evaluate segmentation and credential-tiering controls against it.
